promo-nl-dead.title: Export a JPG and every link is a picture #shorts
promo-nl-dead.description:
Here is a headline with a link on it. In the Canva editor it works — you can click it right now. That is exactly why nobody catches this.

Download. JPG. Open it, click the headline — nothing. There is no link in it, there never was, and nothing in that export dialog warned me.

Canva's help page says it outright: "Image formats like JPG and PNG do not support hyperlinks regardless of the image source."

So PDF instead. Download, PDF Standard, open it, click the headline — it works. PDF is the only export that keeps them.

promo-nl-flatten.title: The Canva fix that kills every link #shorts
promo-nl-flatten.description:
Same PDF that worked a moment ago — and I tick flatten, because my fonts looked wrong on somebody else's computer and flatten is what Canva recommends for that.

Download. Click the headline. Dead.

Flattening merges every layer into one image. Your links were layers. Canva's own wording: it "converts your design with multiple layers into one" and "ensures fonts display accurately".

So the fix for the fonts is the thing that kills the links — and nothing says so. Not the export dialog, not the file. Leave flatten off and export twice instead.

promo-nl-dpi.title: Ninety-six or three hundred? #shorts
promo-nl-dpi.description:
There are two PDF options in that dialog and they are not the same file.

Canva's help page: PDF Standard is 96 dpi, "for illustrations, text, and graphics". PDF Print is 300 dpi, "with bleed, crop marks, and color profile (RGB or CMYK) selection option".

96 is a screen resolution. If your newsletter is emailed as an attachment and read on a laptop, Standard is correct and the file is smaller — which matters when you are attaching it.

But school, church and community newsletters all get printed, and Standard comes out soft and slightly muddy with no fixing it afterwards. So you often need both. Same design, two downloads, thirty seconds.

promo-nl-phone.title: Shrink it to a playing card before you send #shorts
promo-nl-phone.description:
A PDF on a phone is the whole page, zoomed out to fit — so your A4 page arrives about the size of a playing card before anybody pinches to zoom.

So zoom your design out until it is roughly that size and look at it.

What should survive: the masthead, the lead headline, and the shape of the blocks. If your body text has turned into grey stripes, that is fine — that is what body text does.

If your headlines have also turned into grey stripes, they are too small, and nobody will zoom in to find out what they say. And check the top third separately: on a phone that is the whole newsletter until somebody decides to scroll.
